title: Do top-five NFL draft picks actually help bad teams get better?
text:
The NFL Draft Promised Hope, but do the Top-Five Picks Actually Make Bad Teams Better?
For struggling NFL teams, a losing season comes with one prize, a chance to select one of the best college football players in the country. Every spring, fans hope that one early draft pick will change their franchise’s future. Maybe it’s a quarterback who can turn around the offense or maybe it’s even a defensive player who can transform an entire unit.
But what happens when a team keeps getting those opportunities and still struggles to win?
Look at the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Between 2011 and 2025, Jacksonville had top-five selections in nine different drafts. That is more than twice as many draft years as any other team we are analyzing. Yet the Jaguars averaged only about 5.5 regular season wins per year.
That raises a bigger question: Do top-five NFL draft picks actually help bad teams get better?
To investigate, I analyzed NFL draft selections and regular season results from 2011 through 2025. I compared team wins before and during the rookie season of top-five selection, examined franchises that repeatedly drafted near the top and looked at their overall records.
The results suggest that getting a top-five pick can be followed by a dramatic turnaround, but getting those picks repeatedly is no guarantee of long term success.
A Top-Five Pick Can Come Before a Major Turnaround
The first question is simple: Which teams improved the most after making a top-five draft selection?


Code
library(tidyverse)

draft <- read_csv("draft_picks.csv")
games <- read_csv("nfl_game_results_.csv")


topfive <- draft |>
  filter(season >= 2011, season <= 2025) |>
  filter(pick <= 5) |>
  select(season, team, pick)



topfive <- topfive |>
  mutate(
    team = case_when(
      team == "GNB" ~ "GB",
      team ==  "KAN" ~ "KC",
      team == "LAR" ~ "LA",
      team == "STL" ~ "LA",
      team == "LVR" ~ "LV",
      team == "OAK" ~ "LV",
      team == "NOR" ~ "NO",
      team == "NWE" ~ "NE",
      team == "SDG" ~ "LAC",
      team == "SFO" ~ "SF",
      team == "TAM" ~ "TB",
      TRUE ~ team
    ),
  )
games <- games |>
  mutate(
    home_team = case_when(
      home_team == "STL" ~ "LA",
      home_team == "OAK" ~ "LV",
      home_team == "SD" ~ "LAC",
      TRUE ~ home_team
    ),
    away_team = case_when(
      away_team == "STL" ~ "LA",
      away_team == "OAK" ~ "LV",
      away_team == "SD" ~ "LAC",
      TRUE ~ away_team
    )
  )

homewins <- games |>
  filter(game_type == "REG") |>
  filter(home_score >= 0, away_score >= 0) |>
  group_by(season, home_team) |>
  summarise(
    wins = sum(home_score > away_score)
  ) |>
  rename(team = home_team)

awaywins <- games |>
  filter(game_type == "REG") |>
  filter(home_score >= 0, away_score >= 0) |>
  group_by(season, away_team) |>
  summarise(
    wins = sum(away_score > home_score)
  ) |>
  rename(team = away_team)

records <- bind_rows(homewins, awaywins) |>
  group_by(season, team) |>
  summarise(
    wins = sum(wins)
  ) |>
  arrange(team, season) |>
  group_by(team) |>
  mutate(
    previous_year_wins = lag(wins),
    following_year_wins = lead(wins)
  )

topfive <- topfive |>
  group_by(season, team) |>
  summarise(
    pick = min(pick)
  )

draftwins <- records |>
  left_join(topfive, by = c("season", "team")) |>
  filter(is.na(pick) == FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    team_year = paste(team, season),
    change = wins - previous_year_wins
  )

top10 <- draftwins |>
  arrange(desc(change)) |>
  head(10)

ggplot() +
  geom_bar(
    data=top10,
    aes(
      x=reorder(team_year, change),
      weight=change
    ),
    fill="#3a6b8a"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title="Which NFL Teams Improved the Most After a Top-Five Draft Pick?",
    subtitle="Top 10 increases in wins from pre-draft to rookie season, 2011–2025.",
    x="NFL Team and Draft Year",
    y="Increase in Regular-Season Wins",
    caption="Source: NFL Draft Picks and NFL Game Results datasets | By: Anna Reimers"
  ) +
 theme_minimal() +
  theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title.position = "plot"
)









The New England Patriots stand out in the first chart.
After winning just four games in 2024, New England selected offensive tackle Will Campbell with the fourth overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft. The Patriots went on to win 14 regular-season games in 2025, an increase of 10 wins.
That’s the largest single-season improvement in this analysis. Other franchises also experience major turnarounds after making top-five selections. Kansas City in 2013 and San Francisco in 2019 each improved by nine wins compared with the previous season.
These results show how quickly an NFL team’s trajectory can change. A team near the bottom of the standings one year can become a serious contender the next.
But there’s an important catch.
A football team doesn’t improve because of one player alone. Coaching changes, trades, free agent signings, injuries and the development of players already on the roster can all influence the final record.
The Patriots improvement, for example, doesn’t prove that Campbell was responsible for those 10 additional wins.
So while the first chart shows that dramatic improvement is possible, it leaves another question unanswered.
What happens to the teams that keep drafting near the top?
For Some Teams, Draft Early Becomes a Pattern
A top-five pick is supposed to help a franchise move forward. But some teams find themselves back near the top of the draft again and again.
To see whether those repeated opportunities lead to better results, I looked at the five franchises with the most top-five draft years.


Code
library(tidyverse)

repeatteams <- topfive |>
  group_by(team) |>
  summarise(
    topfive_picks = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(topfive_picks)) |>
  head(5)

repeatwins <- draftwins |>
  inner_join(repeatteams, by = "team") |>
  filter(is.na(previous_year_wins) == FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data=repeatwins,
    aes(
      y=reorder(team_year, previous_year_wins),
      yend=reorder(team_year, previous_year_wins),
      x=previous_year_wins,
      xend=wins
    ),
    color="lightgrey",
    linewidth=1.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data=repeatwins,
    aes(
      y=reorder(team_year, previous_year_wins),
      x=previous_year_wins,
      color="Before Draft"
    ),
    size=2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data=repeatwins,
    aes(
      y=reorder(team_year, previous_year_wins),
      x=wins,
      color="Rookie Season"
    ),
    size=2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name="Season",
    values=c(
      "Before Draft"="#D50A0A",
      "Rookie Season"="#013369"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title="Do Repeated Top-Five Draft Picks Help Struggling NFL Teams Improve?",
    subtitle="Wins before and during the draft year, 2011–2025",
    x="Regular Season Wins",
    y="Team and Draft Year",
    caption="Source: NFL Draft Picks and NFL Game Results datasets | By: Anna Reimers"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Each pair of dots compares a team’s regular-season wins before a draft with its wins during the selected player’s rookie season.
The results are anything but truly consistent. Some seasons show clear improvement, while others show little movement or even a decline in wins.
Jacksonville is a particularly revealing example. After winning four games in 2024, the Jaguars improved 13 wins in 2025 and a nine win increase. But the franchise’s other top-five draft years did not produce the same improvement.
The same broader pattern appears among other frequently drafting franchises, including Cleveland, the New York Giants, the New York Jets and Washington.
That’s what makes this chart important. It shows that receiving another high selection doesn’t automatically produce a better record the following season. Even within the same franchise, the results can be dramatically different from one draft year to another.
The draft offers teams an opportunity to improve, whether that opportunity turns into wins is a different question.
Jacksonville Has Had More Chances Than Anyone Else
The final question looks beyond every individual season.
Which teams have spent the most time drafting near the top, and how successful have they been overall.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)


draftcounts <- topfive |>
  group_by(team) |>
  summarise(
    TopFivePicks = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(TopFivePicks)) |>
  head(10)


averagewins <- records |>
  filter(season >= 2011, season <= 2025) |>
  group_by(team) |>
  summarise(
    AvgWins = mean(wins)
  )

top10table <- draftcounts |>
  inner_join(averagewins, by = "team")


top10table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    team = "NFL Team",
    TopFivePicks = "Top-Five Draft Years",
    AvgWins = "Average Wins Per Season"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Some NFL Teams Keep Getting Top-Five Draft Picks",
    subtitle = "The 10 teams with the most top-five draft years from 2011–2025 and their average regular-season wins."
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("By: Anna Reimers  |  Source: NFL Draft Picks and NFL Game Results datasets")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(
      cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
      cell_text(weight = "bold", size = 12)
    )
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#006778"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = team == "JAX"
    )
  )

Jacksonville stands out immediately.
The Jaguars had nine draft years with a top-five selection between 2011 and 2025. The next- highest teams in the table only had four. Despite those repeated opportunities, Jacksonville averaged approximately 5.5 wins per season, so that difference matters.
Cleveland provides an interesting comparison. The Browns had four top-five draft years but also averaged about 5.5 wins per season.
Jacksonville had more than twice as many draft years with top-five selection as Cleveland, yet the two franchises finished with similar average win totals. However the table does not tell us whether individual draft selections were good or bad, it doesn’t mean that the Jaguars never improved.
Instead, it reveals a larger problem. The problem is, repeatedly selecting players near the top of the draft hasn’t translated into consistently strong regular season records for some franchises.
A top five pick might bring talent into an organization, but talent alone doesn’t guarantee victories.
So, Does Drafting in the Top Five Actually Work?
The true answer depends on what success looks like. If success means improving immediately, the first chart provides examples of teams making enormous jumps in wins after top-five selections.
If success means consistently getting better, the overall picture becomes less convincing. The dumbbell chart shows that franchises with repeated high selections don’t improve every time. The table shows that Jacksonville, despite having more top-five draft years than anyone else in the analysis, continued to average relatively a few wins.
There are limitations to these findings. Some top-five picks acquire through trades rather than earned through a team’s own losing record. The analysis also measures team victories, not individual player performance. That being said, it cannot prove whether a draft selection causes a team’s improvement or decline.
Still the larger pattern is revealing.
The NFL Draft gives struggling teams a chance to change their future, but it doesn’t guarantee success.
Some teams turn top-five selections into winning seasons, while others continue to struggle despite repeatedly drafting near the top. Ultimately, where a team picks matters less than what it does with the opportunity that is given to them.
